claim: Tapeworms grow at rates rivaling the fastest-growing metazoan tissues.
source: Tapeworms grow at rates rivaling the fastest-growing metazoan tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Tapeworms shed large parts of their body to propagate.
source: To propagate they shed large parts of their body
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworm biology mentioned in the abstract.

claim: Tapeworms regenerate proglottids as part of normal homeostasis to replace lost tissues.
source: to replace these lost tissues they regenerate proglottids (segments) as part of normal homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement about tapeworm biology supported by the study's findings.

claim: Tapeworm growth and regeneration are fueled by adult somatic stem cells.
source: Their remarkable growth and regeneration are fueled by adult somatic stem cells that have yet to be characterized molecularly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tapeworm adult somatic stem cells have not been characterized molecularly prior to this study.
source: Their remarkable growth and regeneration are fueled by adult somatic stem cells that have yet to be characterized molecularly.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge before this study.

claim: Regenerative potential in H. diminuta is regionally limited to the neck.
source: Using the rat intestinal tapeworm, Hymenolepis diminuta, we find that regenerative potential is regionally limited to the neck
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Head-dependent extrinsic signals create a permissive microenvironment for stem cell-driven regeneration in the neck.
source: where head-dependent extrinsic signals create a permissive microenvironment for stem cell-driven regeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including serial amputation experiments.

claim: There is no evidence that stem cells are restricted to the regeneration-competent neck.
source: We find no evidence that stem cells are restricted to the regeneration-competent neck.
evidence: This is supported by cycling cell distribution data and transplantation experiments.

claim: Lethally irradiated tapeworms can be rescued when cells from regeneration-competent regions are transplanted into the neck.
source: lethally irradiated tapeworms can be rescued when cells from either regeneration-competent or regeneration-incompetent regions are transplanted into the neck.
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Lethally irradiated tapeworms can be rescued when cells from regeneration-incompetent regions are transplanted into the neck.
source: lethally irradiated tapeworms can be rescued when cells from either regeneration-competent or regeneration-incompetent regions are transplanted into the neck.
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The head and neck tissues provide extrinsic cues that regulate stem cells, enabling region-specific regeneration.
source: Together, the head and neck tissues provide extrinsic cues that regulate stem cells, enabling region-specific regeneration in this parasite.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: Tapeworms infect humans and livestock, causing lost economic output, disease, and in rare cases, death.
source: Tapeworms are parasitic flatworms that infect humans and livestock, causing lost economic output, disease, and in rare cases, death (Del Brutto, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Del Brutto, 2013.

claim: Tapeworms are well known for their ability to reach enormous lengths.
source: These parasites are well known for their ability to reach enormous lengths.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworms.

claim: Humans infected with Diphyllobothrium latum harbor parasites that average 6 m in length.
source: For example, humans infected with the broad or fish tapeworm, Diphyllobothrium latum, harbor parasites that average 6 m in length (Craig and Ito, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Craig and Ito, 2007.

claim: Tapeworms can regenerate to accommodate their multi-host life cycle.
source: It is less commonly appreciated that tapeworms can regenerate to accommodate their multi-host life cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworm biology.

claim: Adult tapeworms in their host intestines develop proglottids that are gravid with embryos.
source: Adult tapeworms in their host intestines develop proglottids (segments) that are gravid with embryos.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworm biology.

claim: Tapeworms pinch off the posterior and gravid sections of their body, which exit with the host excrement.
source: Tapeworms pinch off the posterior and gravid sections of their body, which exit with the host excrement, to be eaten by a suitable intermediate host that supports larval tapeworm development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tapeworm life cycle.

claim: Despite losing large body sections, the tapeworm does not progressively shorten.
source: Despite losing large body sections, the tapeworm does not progressively shorten; instead, it regenerates proglottids, allowing the worms to maintain an equilibrium length.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworm biology.

claim: Tapeworms regenerate proglottids, allowing the worms to maintain an equilibrium length.
source: Despite losing large body sections, the tapeworm does not progressively shorten; instead, it regenerates proglottids, allowing the worms to maintain an equilibrium length.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapeworm biology.

claim: H. diminuta was a favorite model organism among parasitologists up to the 1980s.
source: Up to the 1980s the rat intestinal tapeworm, Hymenolepis diminuta, had been a favorite model organism among parasitologists.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the use of H. diminuta in research.

claim: H. diminuta grows rapidly, producing up to 2200 proglottids within the first 15 days of infection.
source: H. diminuta grows rapidly–within the first 15 days of infection, it produces up to 2200 proglottids, increases in length by up to 3400 times, and weight by up to 1.8 million times (Roberts, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts, 1980.

claim: H. diminuta increases in length by up to 3400 times within the first 15 days of infection.
source: H. diminuta grows rapidly–within the first 15 days of infection, it produces up to 2200 proglottids, increases in length by up to 3400 times, and weight by up to 1.8 million times (Roberts, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts, 1980.

claim: H. diminuta increases in weight by up to 1.8 million times within the first 15 days of infection.
source: H. diminuta grows rapidly–within the first 15 days of infection, it produces up to 2200 proglottids, increases in length by up to 3400 times, and weight by up to 1.8 million times (Roberts, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts, 1980.

claim: H. diminuta is easily propagated in the laboratory.
source: H. diminuta grows rapidly–within the first 15 days of infection, it produces up to 2200 proglottids, increases in length by up to 3400 times, and weight by up to 1.8 million times (Roberts, 1980)–and is easily propagated in the laboratory.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H. diminuta.

claim: Foundational work on H. diminuta's biochemistry, ultrastructure, and developmental biology enriched understanding of these tapeworms.
source: Foundational work on their biochemistry, ultrastructure, and developmental biology enriched our understanding of these tapeworms (Arai, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arai, 1980.

claim: With the dawn of the molecular age and the rise of genetic model organisms, H. diminuta was essentially left behind.
source: However, with the dawn of the molecular age and the rise of genetic model organisms, H. diminuta was essentially left behind.
evidence: This is a historical statement about research trends.

claim: H. diminuta is an excellent, tractable model for the study of stem cells and regeneration.
source: Here, we show that H. diminuta is an excellent, tractable model for the study of stem cells and regeneration, with the power to inform us about parasite physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Adult H. diminuta will expire once its host rat dies.
source: As an obligate endoparasite, adult H. diminuta will expire once its host rat dies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about obligate endoparasites.

claim: The lifespan of H. diminuta can be greatly increased via regeneration.
source: However, the lifespan of H. diminuta can be greatly increased via regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation to Read, 1967.

claim: A single adult tapeworm can be serially amputated and transplanted into a new host intestine, where the fragment can regenerate into a mature tapeworm even after 13 rounds of amputation over 14 years.
source: A single adult tapeworm can be serially amputated and transplanted into a new host intestine, where the fragment can regenerate into a mature tapeworm even after 13 rounds of amputation over 14 years (Read, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Read, 1967.

claim: Observations have led to speculation that H. diminuta may be inherently immortal.
source: These observations have led to speculation that H. diminuta may be inherently immortal.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on previous observations.

claim: Freshwater planarians like Schmidtea mediterranea reproduce indefinitely by fission.
source: This situation is reminiscent of the free-living cousins of tapeworms: freshwater planarians like Schmidtea mediterranea, which reproduce indefinitely by fission, and can regenerate their whole body from tiny fragments (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002.

claim: Freshwater planarians like Schmidtea mediterranea can regenerate their whole body from tiny fragments.
source: This situation is reminiscent of the free-living cousins of tapeworms: freshwater planarians like Schmidtea mediterranea, which reproduce indefinitely by fission, and can regenerate their whole body from tiny fragments (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002.

claim: Planarian immortality and regeneration are enabled by adult somatic stem cells called neoblasts.
source: Planarian immortality and regeneration are enabled by adult somatic stem cells called neoblasts (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002; Reddien, 2018; Baguñà, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002; Reddien, 2018; Baguñà, 2012.

claim: Neoblasts are the only dividing undifferentiated cells within the planarian soma.
source: These stem cells are the only dividing undifferentiated cells within the soma.
evidence: This is established knowledge about planarian neoblasts.

claim: H. diminuta maintains a population of neoblast-like adult somatic stem cells.
source: Like planarians, H. diminuta maintains a population of neoblast-like adult somatic stem cells (Roberts, 1980) that are likely responsible for their growth and regenerative ability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts, 1980.

claim: Neoblast-like adult somatic stem cells in H. diminuta are likely responsible for their growth and regenerative ability.
source: Like planarians, H. diminuta maintains a population of neoblast-like adult somatic stem cells (Roberts, 1980) that are likely responsible for their growth and regenerative ability.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with planarians and supported by the study's findings.

claim: Stem cells of multiple species of parasitic flatworms have been described recently.
source: Recently, stem cells of multiple species of parasitic flatworms have been described (Collins et al., 2013; Koziol et al., 2014; Koziol et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013; Koziol et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Stem cells play crucial roles in parasite development, transmission, homeostasis, and disease.
source: Stem cells play crucial roles in parasite development, transmission, homeostasis, and even disease.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent examples and citations.

claim: Stem cells enable prolific reproduction and longevity in parasites.
source: For example, stem cells enable prolific reproduction and longevity (Collins, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collins, 2017.

claim: Stem cells mediate host-parasite interactions.
source: mediate host-parasite interactions (Collins et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2016.

claim: Stem cells allow metastatic parasite transmission in host tissues.
source: and allow metastatic parasite transmission in host tissues (Brehm and Koziol, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brehm and Koziol, 2014.

claim: The anatomy of adult H. diminuta consists of a head with four suckers, an unsegmented neck, and a body with thousands of proglottids/segments.
source: The anatomy of adult H. diminuta consists of a head with four suckers, an unsegmented neck, and a body with thousands of proglottids/segments that grow and mature in an anterior-to-posterior direction (Roberts, 1980; Rozario and Newmark, 2015) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Proglottids in H. diminuta grow and mature in an anterior-to-posterior direction.
source: The anatomy of adult H. diminuta consists of a head with four suckers, an unsegmented neck, and a body with thousands of proglottids/segments that grow and mature in an anterior-to-posterior direction (Roberts, 1980; Rozario and Newmark, 2015) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In vitro culture conditions for H. diminuta were established modified from Schiller's method.
source: We established H. diminuta in vitro culture conditions modified from Schiller's method (Schiller, 1965)
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation.

claim: Anterior-most fragments (head+neck+body) were competent to regenerate.
source: The anterior-most fragments (head+neck+body) were competent to regenerate, confirming in vivo observations using amputation and transplantation (Read, 1967; Goodchild, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Anterior fragments that were first decapitated (neck+body) were competent to regenerate.
source: Anterior fragments that were first decapitated (neck+body) were also competent to regenerate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 'Body only' fragments failed to regenerate proglottids.
source: In contrast, 'body only' fragments failed to regenerate proglottids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: All amputated fragments could grow in length.
source: All amputated fragments could grow in length (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: All amputated fragments could differentiate mature reproductive structures and mate.
source: All amputated fragments could grow in length (Figure 1d), differentiate mature reproductive structures, and mate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: 'Body only' fragments could grow because each existing proglottid increased in length as it progressively matured.
source: Despite the failure to regenerate, 'body only' fragments could grow because each existing proglottid increased in length as it progressively matured (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: Only fragments that retained the neck were able to regenerate new proglottids over time.
source: However, only fragments that retained the neck were able to regenerate new proglottids over time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The neck of 6-day-old tapeworms is typically 2–3 mm long when observed after DAPI staining and widefield fluorescent microscopy.
source: The neck of 6-day-old tapeworms used in this study is typically 2–3 mm long when observed after DAPI staining and widefield fluorescent microscopy.
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: 2 mm 'neck only' fragments regenerate an average of 383 proglottids after 12 days in vitro.
source: By amputating 2 mm 'neck only' fragments, we find that the neck is sufficient to regenerate an average of 383 proglottids (SD = 138, N = 4, n = 20) after 12 days in vitro (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Head regeneration was not observed in any case.
source: In no case did we observe head regeneration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Amputated heads alone could not regenerate in vitro.
source: Furthermore, amputated heads alone could not regenerate in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Amputated heads alone could not regenerate in vivo.
source: Furthermore, amputated heads alone could not regenerate in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) nor in vivo (Read, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Read, 1967.

claim: Neither the head nor body can regenerate proglottids.
source: Thus, neither the head nor body can regenerate proglottids, but the neck is both necessary and sufficient for proglottid-specific regeneration in H. diminuta.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The neck is both necessary and sufficient for proglottid-specific regeneration in H. diminuta.
source: Thus, neither the head nor body can regenerate proglottids, but the neck is both necessary and sufficient for proglottid-specific regeneration in H. diminuta.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Anterior fragments of H. diminuta can regenerate after at least four rounds of serial amputation in vitro.
source: Using in vitro culture, we confirmed that anterior fragments of H. diminuta can regenerate after at least four rounds of serial amputation (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f–g.

claim: Decapitated (-head) fragments regenerated proglottids after the first amputation.
source: Decapitated (-head) fragments regenerated proglottids after the first amputation; however, re-amputation abrogated regeneration (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f–g.

claim: Re-amputation of decapitated fragments abrogated regeneration.
source: Decapitated (-head) fragments regenerated proglottids after the first amputation; however, re-amputation abrogated regeneration (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f–g.

claim: After decapitation, a definitive neck could not be maintained and eventually, the whole tissue was comprised of proglottids.
source: After decapitation, a definitive neck could not be maintained and eventually, the whole tissue was comprised of proglottids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Without the head, proglottid regeneration from the neck is finite.
source: Without the head, proglottid regeneration from the neck is finite.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the serial amputation experiments.

claim: The neck is necessary and sufficient for proglottid regeneration, but the head is required to maintain an unsegmented neck and for persistent regeneration.
source: Thus, while the neck is necessary and sufficient for proglottid regeneration, the head is required to maintain an unsegmented neck and for persistent regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Regeneration potential is asymmetric across the neck A-P axis with a strong anterior bias.
source: We subdivided the neck into three 1 mm fragments and found that the most-anterior neck fragments regenerated more proglottids than the middle or posterior neck fragments (Figure 1h–i). Thus, regeneration potential is asymmetric across the neck A-P axis with a strong anterior bias.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1h–i.

claim: The most-anterior neck fragments regenerated more proglottids than the middle or posterior neck fragments.
source: We subdivided the neck into three 1 mm fragments and found that the most-anterior neck fragments regenerated more proglottids than the middle or posterior neck fragments (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1h–i.

claim: In flatworms, the only proliferative somatic cells are undifferentiated cells with stem cell morphology and/or function.
source: In flatworms, it has been repeatedly shown that the only proliferative somatic cells are undifferentiated cells with stem cell morphology and/or function; these cells have been termed neoblasts, adult somatic stem cells, or germinative cells, depending on the organism (Collins et al., 2013; Koziol et al., 2014; Baguñà et al., 1989; Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2000; Ladurner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In H. diminuta, proliferation does not occur in regions comprised solely of differentiated cells (muscle and tegument/parasite skin at the animal edge).
source: In H. diminuta, proliferation does not occur in regions comprised solely of differentiated cells (muscle and tegument/parasite skin at the animal edge) (Bolla and Roberts, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bolla and Roberts, 1971.

claim: Proliferation in H. diminuta is only detected in regions where undifferentiated cells with the typical morphology of stem cells can be distinguished.
source: Instead, proliferation is only detected in regions where undifferentiated cells with the typical morphology of stem cells can be distinguished (Bolla and Roberts, 1971; Sulgostowska, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bolla and Roberts, 1971 and Sulgostowska, 1972.

claim: Cycling somatic cells in H. diminuta would not include differentiated cells, but would include stem cells and any dividing progeny.
source: Thus, cycling somatic cells in H. diminuta would not include differentiated cells, but would include stem cells and any dividing progeny.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and observations.

claim: mcm2 and h2b are conserved cycling-cell markers in free-living and parasitic flatworms.
source: FISH to detect cell cycle-regulated transcripts, such as the replication licensing factor minichromosome maintenance complex component 2 (mcm2) and histone h2b (h2b), which are conserved cycling-cell markers in free-living and parasitic flatworms (Collins et al., 2013; Solana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2013 and Solana et al., 2012.

claim: Cycling somatic cells were detected throughout the tapeworm body.
source: We detected cycling somatic cells throughout the tapeworm body (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a–b.

claim: Cycling cells were detected in the head, though in small numbers.
source: Contrary to previous results (Bolla and Roberts, 1971), we also detected cycling cells in the head, though in small numbers (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The scarcity of cycling cells in the head may be the reason they were originally missed.
source: The scarcity of these cells may be the reason they were originally missed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation.

claim: Cycling cells are present in all regions, regardless of regeneration competence.
source: Taken together, cycling cells are present in all regions, regardless of regeneration competence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cycling cell distribution data.

claim: Exposing H. diminuta to 200 Gy x-irradiation reduced the number of cycling cells by 91 ± 6% after 3 days.
source: Exposing H. diminuta to 200 Gy x-irradiation reduced the number of cycling cells by 91 ± 6% after 3 days (Figure 2c–d)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2c–d.

claim: 200 Gy x-irradiation abrogated both growth and regeneration in H. diminuta.
source: Exposing H. diminuta to 200 Gy x-irradiation reduced the number of cycling cells by 91 ± 6% after 3 days (Figure 2c–d) and abrogated both growth and regeneration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: 200 Gy x-irradiation is lethal to H. diminuta; all fragments from worms exposed to this dosage degenerated after 1 month.
source: This dosage is lethal; all fragments from worms exposed to 200 Gy x-irradiation degenerated after 1 month (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d.

claim: 683 transcripts were identified as irradiation sensitive (downregulated; FDR ≤ 0.05).
source: We identified 683 transcripts that were irradiation sensitive (downregulated; FDR ≤ 0.05) (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Expression of irradiation-sensitive transcripts by WISH was reduced after exposure to irradiation.
source: Expression of irradiation-sensitive transcripts by WISH was indeed reduced after exposure to irradiation, validating our RNA-seq approach (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cycling cells reside in the neck parenchyma bounded by the nerve cords and are absent from the animal edge where muscle and tegument are located.
source: The position of cycling cells in the neck is spatially restricted in a conserved pattern (Koziol and Castillo, 2011) (Figure 3a): cycling cells reside in the neck parenchyma bounded by the nerve cords and are absent from the animal edge where muscle and tegument are located (Bolla and Roberts, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Among 194 irradiation-sensitive transcripts that displayed clear WISH patterns, 63% were expressed in the neck parenchyma.
source: Among 194 irradiation-sensitive transcripts that displayed clear WISH patterns, 63% were expressed in the neck parenchyma, though in a variety of patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 13% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts showed similar patterns to h2b and mcm2.
source: 13% showed similar patterns to h2b and mcm2 (Figure 3b–c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3b–c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: zmym3, pogzl, nab2, and lbr are irradiation-sensitive transcripts with expression patterns similar to h2b and mcm2.
source: These include the predicted nucleic acid binding factors Zn finger MYM type 3 (zmym3) and pogo transposable element with ZN finger domain-like (pogzl), as well as NAB co-repressor domain two superfamily member (nab2) and nuclear lamina component laminB receptor (lbr).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: 25% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts were expressed in a minority of cells in the neck parenchyma.
source: 25% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts, were expressed in a minority of cells in the neck parenchyma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: 24% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts were expressed within the parenchyma and more broadly toward the animal edge.
source: 24% were expressed within the parenchyma and more broadly toward the animal edge (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: All transcripts that were expressed in the neck parenchyma were also found throughout the worm body, even in the most posterior proglottids.
source: All transcripts that were expressed in the neck parenchyma were also found throughout the worm body, even in the most posterior proglottids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: Irradiation-sensitive transcripts identified by RNA-seq likely represent markers for stem cells, progenitors, and even differentiated cells that were lost or compromised following irradiation.
source: In conclusion, irradiation-sensitive transcripts identified by RNA-seq likely represent markers for stem cells, progenitors, and even differentiated cells that were lost or compromised following irradiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: zmym3, pogzl, nab2, and lbr were co-expressed in cycling somatic cells.
source: The irradiation-sensitive transcripts from Figure 3c were indeed colocalized in cycling somatic cells (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: prox1 was expressed exclusively in a subset of cycling cells.
source: One transcript, the homeobox factor prospero (prox1), was expressed exclusively in a subset of cycling cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: HDt_10981 and ppt1 were expressed in both cycling cells and non-cycling cells.
source: We confirmed that genes with expression that only partially overlapped in the neck parenchyma, such as the Zn finger-containing gene HDt_10981 and palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (ppt1), were expressed in both cycling cells and non-cycling cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Genes like HDt_10981 and ppt1 likely represent lineage-committed stem cells or progenitors for tissues such as muscle, neurons, tegument, or protonephridia.
source: We propose that these genes likely represent lineage-committed stem cells or progenitors for tissues such as muscle, neurons, tegument, or protonephridia.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: 28% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts were predominantly expressed in non-cycling cells that were juxtaposed to cycling cells.
source: 28% of irradiation-sensitive transcripts were predominantly expressed in non-cycling cells that were juxtaposed to cycling cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The transcriptional heterogeneity detected in the cycling-cell compartment is reminiscent of similar observations made in the regenerative planarian S. mediterranea.
source: The transcriptional heterogeneity detected in the cycling-cell compartment is reminiscent of similar observations made in the regenerative planarian S. mediterranea (Reddien, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by a citation to Reddien, 2018.

claim: A comparative analysis revealed a number of transcripts with conserved expression in cycling-cell populations from tapeworms and planarians.
source: A comparative analysis between verified tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts and their putative planarian homologs revealed a number of transcripts with conserved expression in cycling-cell populations from these distantly related flatworms (Supplementary file 1c)
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Knockdown of h2b, zmym3, and pogzl each resulted in diminished growth and regeneration.
source: Knockdown of h2b, zmym3, and pogzl each resulted in diminished growth and regeneration (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 4b–c.

claim: RNAi knockdown of h2b, zmym3, and pogzl severely reduced the number of proliferative cells in the neck that could incorporate F-ara-EdU.
source: RNAi knockdown of h2b, zmym3, and pogzl severely reduced the number of proliferative cells in the neck that could incorporate F-ara-EdU (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4d–e.

claim: Fewer mcm2+ cells were observed after RNAi of h2b, zmym3, and pogzl.
source: We also observed fewer mcm2+ cells after RNAi (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: h2b, zmym3, and pogzl are necessary for the maintenance and/or proper function of cycling cells, likely including stem cells, in H. diminuta.
source: Therefore, h2b, zmym3, and pogzl are necessary for the maintenance and/or proper function of cycling cells, likely including stem cells, in H. diminuta.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi data.

claim: All cycling-cell transcripts including zmym3 and pogzl were detected throughout the whole tapeworm body by WISH and FISH.
source: By WISH and FISH, all cycling-cell transcripts including zmym3 and pogzl were detected throughout the whole tapeworm body (Figure 4g, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is supported by WISH and FISH data shown in Figure 4g and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: In the tapeworm posterior, zmym3 and pogzl were expressed in gonadal tissues and in somatic cells within the parenchyma.
source: In the tapeworm posterior, zmym3 and pogzl were expressed in gonadal tissues (which contain mitotic germ cells) but also in somatic cells within the parenchyma (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 461 anterior-enriched and 241 anterior-depleted transcripts were identified by RNA-seq of neck fragments.
source: Thus, we performed RNA-seq of 1 mm anterior, middle, and posterior neck fragments (Figure 1h), and identified 461 anterior-enriched and 241 anterior-depleted transcripts (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: Anterior-enriched and anterior-depleted transcripts were often detected in corresponding gradients by WISH.
source: By WISH, anterior-enriched and anterior-depleted transcripts were often detected in corresponding gradients (Figure 5a)
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The majority of anterior-enriched transcripts (88%) were not irradiation sensitive.
source: When we overlaid the anterior-enriched and -depleted datasets with our irradiation-sensitive dataset, the majority of anterior-enriched transcripts (88%) were not irradiation sensitive (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The A-P polarized signals across the neck region arise predominantly within the non-cycling compartments.
source: Our results suggest that the A-P polarized signals across the neck region arise predominantly within the non-cycling compartments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and WISH data.

claim: 57 transcripts were anterior enriched and irradiation sensitive by RNA-seq.
source: Since our RNA-seq analysis identified 57 transcripts that were anterior enriched and irradiation sensitive, we examined expression patterns within this category.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 15 transcripts that were anterior enriched and irradiation sensitive were expressed in a subset of cells within the neck parenchyma.
source: We found 15 transcripts expressed in a subset of cells within the neck parenchyma (Figure 5c)
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The majority (7/8) of anterior-enriched transcripts tested by dFISH were not expressed in cycling cells.
source: We were able to successfully test eight candidates by dFISH with cycling-cell markers and found that the majority (7/8) were not expressed in cycling cells (Figure 5d, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 5d and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Only prox1 among anterior-enriched transcripts was co-expressed in cycling cells.
source: Only prox1 was co-expressed in cycling cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: prox1 is expressed throughout the tapeworm body.
source: Furthermore, prox1 is expressed throughout the tapeworm body (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The analyses have not revealed an anteriorly biased subpopulation of stem cells that confer regenerative ability.
source: Thus, our analyses have not revealed an anteriorly biased subpopulation of stem cells that confer regenerative ability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and expression analysis data.

claim: Bulk-cell transplants were able to either partially or fully rescue irradiated worms that were destined to die.
source: Remarkably, bulk-cell transplants were able to either partially or fully rescue irradiated worms that were destined to die (Figure 6a,c).
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation data shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: No proglottid regeneration was observed in irradiated worms with or without buffer injection.
source: We did not observe any proglottid regeneration in irradiated worms with or without buffer injection (Figure 6a,c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: Large colonies of F-ara-EdU+ cells could be detected 3 days post-transplantation.
source: Despite this issue, we were able to detect large colonies of F-ara-EdU+ cells 3 days post-transplantation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Some labeled cells from donors were incorporated into terminally differentiated tissues at the animal edge.
source: We also observed that some labeled cells were incorporated into terminally differentiated tissues at the animal edge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d: inset).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Cycling cells from donors are able to become established and differentiate inside the irradiated host.
source: Thus, cycling cells from donors are able to become established and differentiate inside the irradiated host.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transplantation data.

claim: 50 mM hydroxyurea (HU) treatment resulted in 96 ± 3% loss of cycling cells after 6 days.
source: To test if the cycling-cell population is necessary to rescue lethally irradiated tapeworms, we depleted cycling cells from donor worms using 50 mM hydroxyurea (HU), which resulted in 96 ± 3% loss of cycling cells after 6 days (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e–f.

claim: Cycling cells are essential for rescue of regeneration as injected cells from HU-treated donors rescued only 1% of the time.
source: Cycling cells are essential for rescue of regeneration as injected cells from HU-treated donors rescued only 1% of the time, compared to 26% rescue using cells sourced from sister donors that did not receive the drug (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6b–c.

claim: Tapeworm cycling cells contain bona fide stem cell activity.
source: Our results suggest that tapeworm cycling cells contain bona fide stem cell activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transplantation experiments.

claim: Cells from either anterior donor tissues or posterior donor tissues were able to rescue regeneration in lethally irradiated tapeworms.
source: With this functional assay in hand, we examined the rescue ability of cells from anterior donor tissues (including the regeneration-competent neck) compared to donor tissues from the most posterior termini of 6-day-old tapeworms (which are regeneration incompetent and exclusively comprised of proglottids). Cells from either region were able to rescue regeneration in lethally irradiated tapeworms (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6b–c.

claim: Cells from posterior proglottids were competent to receive signals from the head and neck region that regulate regenerative ability.
source: Thus, cells from posterior proglottids were competent to receive signals from the head and neck region that regulate regenerative ability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transplantation data.

claim: Cycling cells from tapeworm posteriors can give rise to multiple differentiated cell types like muscle/tegument at the animal edge as well as flame cells of the protonephridial system.
source: Interestingly, using pulse-chase experiments with F-ara-EdU, we find that the cycling cells of posterior proglottids can give rise to multiple differentiated cell types like muscle/tegument at the animal edge as well as flame cells of the protonephridial system marked by anti-acetylated α-tubulin antibodies (Rozario and Newmark, 2015) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cycling cells from tapeworm posteriors show hallmarks of stem cell activity, despite the fact that this tissue is not competent to regenerate.
source: Thus, the cycling cells from tapeworm posteriors show hallmarks of stem cell activity, despite the fact that this tissue is not competent to regenerate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pulse-chase and transplantation data.

claim: The regeneration competence of the neck is due to extrinsic signals that regulate regeneration, rather than intrinsic properties of stem cells in the neck region.
source: Taken together, the results of our study support the idea that the regeneration competence of the neck is due to extrinsic signals that regulate regeneration, rather than intrinsic properties of stem cells in the neck region (see Discussion).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: The head and neck environment provide cues that regulate the ability of stem cells to regenerate proglottids.
source: It appears that in tapeworms, location matters enormously: the head and neck environment provide cues that regulate the ability of stem cells to regenerate proglottids, even though cycling cells (and likely stem cells), are not anatomically confined.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cycling cells (and likely stem cells) are not anatomically confined in tapeworms.
source: It appears that in tapeworms, location matters enormously: the head and neck environment provide cues that regulate the ability of stem cells to regenerate proglottids, even though cycling cells (and likely stem cells), are not anatomically confined.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cycling cell distribution and transplantation data.

claim: Both free-living and parasitic flatworms maintain stem cells throughout adulthood but display a range of regenerative abilities.
source: Across the flatworm phylum, both free-living and parasitic worms maintain stem cells throughout adulthood but display a range of regenerative abilities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flatworm biology.

claim: The blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni cannot regenerate after amputation.
source: The blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni cannot regenerate after amputation, though it does employ adult somatic stem cells in other ways, such as to repair injury (Collins and Collins, 2016) and maintain its tegument (Collins et al., 2016; Wendt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Schistosoma mansoni employs adult somatic stem cells to repair injury.
source: The blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni cannot regenerate after amputation, though it does employ adult somatic stem cells in other ways, such as to repair injury (Collins and Collins, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collins and Collins, 2016.

claim: Schistosoma mansoni employs adult somatic stem cells to maintain its tegument.
source: The blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni cannot regenerate after amputation, though it does employ adult somatic stem cells in other ways, such as to repair injury (Collins and Collins, 2016) and maintain its tegument (Collins et al., 2016; Wendt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2016 and Wendt et al., 2018.

claim: The regenerative ability of tapeworms had never been tested comprehensively prior to this study.
source: Prior to this study, the regenerative ability of tapeworms had never been tested comprehensively.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge before this study.

claim: Anterior fragments containing the head, neck, and immature proglottids could regenerate into fully mature tapeworms once transplanted into a rat intestine.
source: Although it was known that anterior fragments containing the head, neck, and immature proglottids could regenerate into fully mature tapeworms once transplanted into a rat intestine (Read, 1967; Goodchild, 1958)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Read, 1967 and Goodchild, 1958.

claim: Fragments lacking heads could not be tested for regenerative ability using transplantation.
source: fragments lacking heads could not be tested for regenerative ability using transplantation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Attempts to suture H. diminuta fragments with mutilated or removed heads into a rat intestine resulted in these fragments being invariably flushed out.
source: Attempts were made to suture H. diminuta fragments with mutilated or removed heads into a rat intestine but these fragments were invariably flushed out (Goodchild, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goodchild, 1958.

claim: A robust in vitro culture system allowed testing of regeneration of any amputated H. diminuta fragment for the first time.
source: Here we employ a robust in vitro culture system that allowed us to test regeneration of any amputated H. diminuta fragment for the first time.
evidence: This is a methodological advance described in the study.

claim: During homeostasis, the neck of H. diminuta serves as a 'growth zone' from which proglottids are thought to bud one at a time.
source: During homeostasis, the neck of H. diminuta serves as a 'growth zone' from which proglottids are thought to bud one at a time (Lumsden and Specian, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lumsden and Specian, 1980.

claim: Cells with the typical morphology of stem cells reside in the neck of H. diminuta.
source: Furthermore, cells with the typical morphology of stem cells reside in the neck (Bolla and Roberts, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bolla and Roberts, 1971.

claim: Irradiation may have secondary effects beyond stem cell depletion.
source: Though irradiation may have secondary effects beyond stem cell depletion (Solana et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Solana et al., 2012.

claim: 38 transcripts were verified to be expressed at least partially in cycling cells using dFISH.
source: Using dFISH, we were able to verify 38 transcripts that were expressed at least partially in cycling cells, providing the first molecular characterization of this population in H. diminuta.
evidence: This is supported by the dFISH data presented in the study.

claim: Parasitic flatworms have lost some stem cell genes (e.g. piwi, vasa, and tudor).
source: However, parasitic flatworms have lost some stem cell genes (e.g. piwi, vasa, and tudor) (Tsai et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2013.

claim: Parasitic flatworms have retained some stem cell genes (e.g. argonaute, fgfr).
source: but retained others (e.g. argonaute, fgfr) (Collins et al., 2013; Koziol et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2013 and Koziol et al., 2014.

claim: Of 38 verified tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts, 28 had putative planarian homologs.
source: Of 38 verified tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts, 28 had putative planarian homologs (tblasx E-value <10−10) though not all were reciprocal blast hits.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: 16 of the putative planarian homologs were designated as cluster-defining genes in the Fincher et al. single-cell sequencing dataset.
source: 16 of these planarian transcripts were designated as cluster-defining genes in the Fincher et al. single-cell sequencing dataset and 6/16 are neoblast cluster-defining genes.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published planarian data.

claim: 6 of the putative planarian homologs are neoblast cluster-defining genes.
source: 16 of these planarian transcripts were designated as cluster-defining genes in the Fincher et al. single-cell sequencing dataset and 6/16 are neoblast cluster-defining genes.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published planarian data.

claim: 22/28 putative planarian homologs of tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts show enriched expression in either the X1 or X2 populations, which contain neoblasts.
source: We find that 22/28 putative planarian homologs of tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts show enriched expression in either the X1 or X2 populations, which contain neoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published planarian FACS data.

claim: Despite >500 million years of separation between free-living and parasitic flatworm evolution, tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts have conserved signatures with planarian neoblasts.
source: Thus, despite >500 million years of separation between free-living and parasitic flatworm evolution (Laumer et al., 2015), tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts have conserved signatures with planarian neoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative analysis and supported by a citation to Laumer et al., 2015.

claim: In multiple species of flatworms, stem cells have been shown to be transcriptionally heterogenous.
source: In multiple species of flatworms, stem cells have been shown to be transcriptionally heterogenous (Solana et al., 2012; Fincher et al., 2018; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In larvae of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, many putative stem cell markers show limited overlapping gene expression patterns.
source: For example, in larvae of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, many putative stem cell markers show limited overlapping gene expression patterns (Koziol et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koziol et al., 2014.

claim: zmym3 and pogzl are neoblast cluster-defining genes in planarians.
source: Both zmym3 and pogzl are neoblast cluster-defining genes in planarians (Supplementary file 1c)
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The functions of zmym3 and pogzl in stem cell regulation may be conserved across tapeworms and planarians.
source: Both zmym3 and pogzl are neoblast cluster-defining genes in planarians (Supplementary file 1c) suggesting that their functions in stem cell regulation may be conserved across the two species.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the comparative data.

claim: The planarian homolog of tapeworm pogzl, factor initiating regeneration 1 (fir1), was shown to be expressed in planarian neoblasts.
source: In fact, the planarian homolog of tapeworm pogzl, factor initiating regeneration 1 (fir1), was recently shown to be expressed in planarian neoblasts (Han, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Han, 2018.

claim: RNAi of fir1 in planarians resulted in decreased cell division after amputation and failure to regenerate blastemas.
source: RNAi of fir1 resulted in decreased cell division after amputation and failure to regenerate blastemas (Han, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Han, 2018.

claim: In other systems, zmym3 regulates cell cycle progression.
source: On the other hand, the function of zmym3 in regeneration is not known, but in other systems, zmym3 regulates cell cycle progression (Hu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2017.

claim: In other systems, zmym3 regulates DNA repair.
source: On the other hand, the function of zmym3 in regeneration is not known, but in other systems, zmym3 regulates cell cycle progression (Hu et al., 2017) and DNA repair (Leung et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leung et al., 2017.

claim: Both zmym3 and pogzl are Zn finger proteins with predicted DNA-binding activity.
source: Coincidentally, both zmym3 and pogzl are Zn finger proteins with predicted DNA-binding activity and could function as transcriptional regulators of stem cells.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prediction.

claim: zmym3 and pogzl could function as transcriptional regulators of stem cells.
source: Coincidentally, both zmym3 and pogzl are Zn finger proteins with predicted DNA-binding activity and could function as transcriptional regulators of stem cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on their predicted properties.

claim: This study showed the first use of RNAi in H. diminuta.
source: In this study, we showed the first use of RNAi in H. diminuta.
evidence: This is a methodological advance described in the study.

claim: RNAi has been demonstrated previously in other tapeworm species.
source: RNAi has been demonstrated previously in other tapeworm species (Pierson et al., 2010; Mizukami et al., 2010; Spiliotis et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pierson et al., 2010; Mizukami et al., 2010; Spiliotis et al., 2010.

claim: RNAi has not been widely adopted for studying tapeworm biology due to technical challenges like poor knockdown efficacy, inefficient penetrance, and the difficulty of in vitro culture.
source: though it has not been widely adopted for studying tapeworm biology due to technical challenges like poor knockdown efficacy, inefficient penetrance, and the difficulty of in vitro culture.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Head regeneration was induced in three naturally regeneration-deficient planarian species by manipulating the gradient of Wnt signaling by RNAi.
source: Head regeneration was induced in three naturally regeneration-deficient planarian species by manipulating the gradient of Wnt signaling by RNAi (Sikes and Newmark, 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Umesono et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sikes and Newmark, 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Umesono et al., 2013.

claim: These planarians maintain pluripotent stem cells but do not normally regenerate heads from posterior tissues due to inappropriately high levels of Wnt signaling, which inhibit anterior regeneration.
source: These planarians maintain pluripotent stem cells but do not normally regenerate heads from posterior tissues due to inappropriately high levels of Wnt signaling, which inhibit anterior regeneration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about planarian regeneration supported by the cited studies.

claim: Gradients of Wnt signaling delineate A-P polarity in tapeworms.
source: As in planarians, gradients of Wnt signaling delineate A-P polarity in tapeworms (Koziol et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koziol et al., 2016.

claim: Transcriptional profiling of the neck A-P axis revealed hundreds of candidate genes with polarized expression profiles.
source: Our transcriptional profiling of the neck A-P axis has already revealed hundreds of candidate genes with polarized expression profiles.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data presented in the study.

claim: Head-dependent signals may create gradients across the neck that inhibit proglottidization and are necessary to maintain the neck as an unsegmented tissue.
source: Head-dependent signals may create gradients across the neck that inhibit proglottidization and are necessary to maintain the neck as an unsegmented tissue.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Proglottids can only form once the inhibitory signals are sufficiently diminished.
source: Proglottids can only form once the inhibitory signals are sufficiently diminished (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In the proposed model, the neck is competent to regenerate because of its juxtaposition to the head.
source: In this model, the neck is competent to regenerate because of its juxtaposition to the head.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: After decapitation, the head-dependent signals eventually dissipate and segmentation signals dominate at the expense of the neck.
source: After decapitation, the head-dependent signals eventually dissipate and segmentation signals dominate at the expense of the neck.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: The head may regulate a niche (directly or indirectly) that is necessary for the maintenance of pluripotency in the neck.
source: The head may regulate a niche (directly or indirectly) that is necessary for the maintenance of pluripotency in the neck.
evidence: This is a proposed model shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In one proposed model, stem cells are collectively pluripotent only when they receive head-dependent niche signals, thus limiting regenerative potential to the neck.
source: In this model, stem cells are collectively pluripotent only when they receive head-dependent niche signals, thus limiting regenerative potential to the neck.
evidence: This is a proposed model shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In an alternative proposed model, stem cells may depend on a local niche that is independent of the head.
source: Alternatively, stem cells may depend on a local niche that is independent of the head.
evidence: This is an alternative proposed model shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In the alternative model, stem cells have the capacity to form all cell lineages from any amputated fragment; however, the extrinsic signals that activate proglottid formation are restricted to the posterior neck region.
source: In this model, stem cells have the capacity to form all cell lineages from any amputated fragment; however, the extrinsic signals that activate proglottid formation are restricted to the posterior neck region.
evidence: This is part of the alternative proposed model shown in Figure 6e.

claim: H. diminuta is a powerful developmental model for understanding intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of stem cells and regeneration.
source: Our study shows that H. diminuta is a powerful developmental model for understanding intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of stem cells and regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the work presented in the study.

claim: H. diminuta can be exploited to understand the complexities of stem cell regulation in parasites.
source: The regionally limited regenerative biology of H. diminuta and the technical advances put forth in this work show that we can exploit this tapeworm to understand the complexities of stem cell regulation in parasites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the work presented in the study.

claim: Heterogenous stem cells in H. diminuta are collectively pluripotent but require extrinsic head-dependent signals to enable persistent proglottid regeneration.
source: We defined heterogenous stem cells that are collectively pluripotent but that require extrinsic head-dependent signals to enable persistent proglottid regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Understanding how the stem cell niche is regulated may have broad implications for elucidating stem cell biology in parasitic flatworms, as well as other regenerative animals.
source: Understanding how the stem cell niche we describe is regulated may have broad implications for elucidating stem cell biology in parasitic flatworms, as well as other regenerative animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the findings.
